Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Stupig keyboard-layout DLL (kbdus1.dll/a.dll) loaded into winlogon.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the Stupig pre-login backdoor loading its trojanized keyboard-layout DLL into winlogon.exe at boot. The module masquerades as the legitimate US-English layout kbdus.dll but is named kbdus1.dll (or a.dll), giving an operator SYSTEM command execution from the logon screen before any sign-in. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade filenames (kbdus1.dll/a.dll vs legit kbdus.dll) plus the winlogon.exe load context and the Symantec-confirmed SHA256 5bb5cff... winlogon loading any keyboard DLL other than kbdus.dll is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against Symantec/security.com which confirmed the DLL names and hash. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-can-type-a-secret-username-at-the-windows-login-screen/
ATT&CKT1547.004 T1036.005
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party IME/keyboard-layout software installing a non-Microsoft layout DLL under an unusual name
  • Legitimate multilingual layout DLLs (kbdusx.dll, kbdusl.dll) if the analyst broadens the name match
  • In-house accessibility tooling that hooks the logon desktop
  • Security product that injects a helper module into winlogon.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (SHA256 in~ ("") ) // retain hash TP; to suppress known-good OEM IME add: and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "winlogon.exe"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the loaded module path/hash; compare SHA256 against 5bb5cff... and verify the DLL is NOT the signed Microsoft kbdus.dll (check signer + FolderPath). 2. Contain: isolate the host — the DLL grants pre-auth SYSTEM shell; do not simply reboot (persistence reloads at startup). Capture memory before power actions. 3. Hunt: on the same host look for srt64.sys (Daxin driver), the Keyboard Layouts registry registration, and winlogon.exe spawning cmd/powershell; sweep the fleet for the same DLL name/hash.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "winlogon.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("kbdus1.dll","a.dll")
    or SHA256 == "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256

id: 6f2a1c84-7b03-4e9a-9d21-4c7e8b6a1f30
description: Detects winlogon.exe loading a keyboard-layout DLL masquerading as kbdus.dll (Stupig backdoor named kbdus1.dll or a.dll)
references:
  - https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/daxin-resurfaces-in-taiwan-alongside.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1547.004
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\winlogon.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\kbdus1.dll'
      - '\a.dll'
  condition: selection
level: high
Malicious keyboard-layout registration pointing to Stupig DLL AIInstallation High
Detects Stupig establishing persistence by registering itself as a keyboard-layout provider so win32k.sys loads it into winlogon.exe. Fires when the 'Layout File' value under the Keyboard Layouts registry key is set to the malicious kbdus1.dll or a.dll instead of a legitimate Microsoft layout binary. Rationale: Anchors on the article's persistence mechanism (keyboard-layout provider registration causing win32k.sys to load the DLL into winlogon.exe) with the concrete malicious value data kbdus1.dll/a.dll. Legit layouts never point 'Layout File' at these names. Symantec/security.com corroborated the registration path and filenames. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig • https://gbhackers.com/stupig-system-level-malware/
ATT&CKT1547.004 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom or OEM keyboard-layout packages that ship a vendor DLL and register a Layout File value
  • Enterprise imaging/GPO that provisions additional input languages at first boot
  • A benign in-house DLL that happens to be named a.dll referenced by a layout entry
  • Localization testing labs installing many non-standard layouts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tiptsf.dll","input.dll") and RegistryValueData !has "kbdus.dll"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full RegistryKey (the layout ID subkey) and the initiating process — legitimate registration is done by system installers, not user processes; validate the referenced DLL's signer/hash. 2. Contain: isolate host, back up the registry hive, and remove the malicious layout entry only after forensic capture (loaded module stays resident in winlogon until reboot). 3. Hunt: correlate to the winlogon.exe DLL load (UC1), the srt64.sys driver, and any winlogon-spawned shells; sweep fleet registries for Layout File values referencing kbdus1.dll/a.dll.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Keyboard Layouts\"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Layout File"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("kbdus1.dll","a.dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Keyboard Layouts\"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Layout File"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("kbdus1.dll","a.dll")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Stupig Backdoor Keyboard-Layout Registry Registration
id: b1d4e7a2-3c56-49f8-8a10-2f9c7d5e6b41
description: Detects a Keyboard Layouts 'Layout File' value pointing to the Stupig DLL (kbdus1.dll/a.dll) used for winlogon.exe persistence
references:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 (@TargetObject:*\\Keyboard?Layouts\\* OR @TargetObject:*\\keyboard?layouts\\*) (@Details:*kbdus1.dll* OR @Details:*kbdus1.DLL* OR @Details:*\\a.dll* OR @Details:*\\A.DLL*)

| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Control\\Keyboard Layouts\\*" AND Registry.registry_value_name="Layout File" AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*kbdus1.dll*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\a.dll*") by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
winlogon.exe spawning a command shell (Stupig pre-login SYSTEM execution) AIExploitation High
Detects the Stupig backdoor's payoff behaviour: after a 'stupig'-prefixed username is entered at the logon screen, the DLL running inside winlogon.exe spawns cmd.exe/PowerShell (or runs a command) as SYSTEM on the secure desktop. winlogon.exe is not a normal parent for interactive shells or recon tools. Rationale: Directly targets the article's described payoff — Stupig inside winlogon.exe spawning a SYSTEM cmd on the logon screen. winlogon's only legitimate children are userinit.exe/LogonUI.exe/fontdrvhost/dwm, so a shell or recon binary child is a high-fidelity SYSTEM-escalation signal independent of hashes. Behaviour confirmed across security.com and cybersecuritynews. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-can-type-a-secret-username-at-the-windows-login-screen/
ATT&CKT1547.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint security/EDR validation tooling that intentionally spawns processes from winlogon during red-team tests
  • Legacy accessibility utilities or third-party credential providers launching helpers on the secure desktop
  • Some remote-assistance products injecting a shell into the logon session
  • Broken driver/OEM software mis-parenting a process to winlogon
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\Windows\\System32\\oobe\\","BdeUISrv"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine and integrity level (expect SYSTEM) — a command line following the shell often reveals the operator's action; check who was physically/RDP at console. 2. Contain: isolate host and capture volatile memory before reboot (Stupig persists via the layout DLL). 3. Hunt: pivot to the kbdus1.dll/a.dll load and layout registration on the same host, look for srt64.sys, and review downstream child processes (net/whoami/reg) for lateral-movement recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "winlogon.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","reg.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\winlogon.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\net.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\net1.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\whoami.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TokenElevationType, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

Daxin kernel rootkit driver srt64.sys drop / service install AIInstallation High
Detects installation of the Daxin kernel-mode rootkit as srt64.sys under System32\drivers, matched by name/path and the Symantec-confirmed SHA256. Daxin registers as a signed kernel driver, hijacks existing TCP connections for covert C2, and can reach air-gapped segments via multi-hop. Rationale: Uses the article's exact driver name/path (%SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\srt64.sys) and the Symantec-verified SHA256 49c827... The 7045 angle catches the kernel-driver service registration Daxin requires. Corroborated by security.com's 2026 report and the original 2022 Symantec Daxin analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig • https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/daxin-backdoor-espionage
ATT&CKT1014 T1543.003 T1205
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated legitimate drivers with similar short names (e.g. Symantec srtsp64.sys) if the analyst loosens the name match — the exact 'srt64.sys' + drivers path is specific
  • Backup/EDR agents installing kernel drivers during a maintenance window (distinguishable by signer and expected name)
  • Driver-signing test/QA machines loading many unsigned/renamed .sys files
  • Forensic/IR tooling dropping a driver by copy into drivers\ during response
Suppression filter
| where FileName =~ "srt64.sys" and FolderPath has @"\System32\drivers\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccsvchst.exe","smc.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the file hash against 49c827... and inspect the driver's Authenticode signer/timestamp (Daxin carries a 2013 compile stamp) and the creating process. 2. Contain: isolate host from all network segments — Daxin hijacks existing TCP sessions and supports multi-hop to air-gapped hosts, so conventional egress blocking is insufficient; capture memory, then plan an offline reimage. 3. Hunt: check for Stupig co-infection (kbdus1.dll/a.dll, Keyboard Layouts registration, winlogon shell), review the host's TCP peers for downstream multi-hop victims, and sweep the fleet for the srt64.sys name/hash and matching 2013 compile timestamps.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where (FileName =~ "srt64.sys" and FolderPath has @"\System32\drivers\")
    or SHA256 == "49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceFileName has "srt64.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f") or SHA1 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f") or MD5 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f") or SHA1 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f") or MD5 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Article-specific bespoke detection — Daxin Resurfaces in Taiwan Alongside Stupig Pre-Login SYSTEM Backdoor
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named

DeviceProcessEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine

// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,

UAT-11795 mshta.exe ClickFix HTA stager fetching from Starland staging domains AIDelivery High
Hunts mshta.exe launching a weaponized HTA whose command line or outbound connection references UAT-11795 staging/C2 domains (zynaris.io, eorthopaedics.com, sastoro.com, web-devtools.com). This is the ClickFix-delivered initial-access stage that pulls the trojanized installer and byte-compiled Python loader. Rationale: Anchors on mshta.exe (LOLBIN) plus the exact UAT-11795 staging/C2 domains from the article — the domain literals make this near-zero FP versus generic mshta hunting. Cross-checked BleepingComputer and CyberPress write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://cyberpress.org/uat-11795-spreads-dual-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1204.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Threat-intel analyst pasting the IOC domain into a test HTA
  • Red-team engagement replaying the ClickFix lure
  • Web-filtering/proxy test tools embedding the domain string in an mshta test
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cmd.exe") or true // keep all; refine by excluding known sandbox device groups: | where DeviceName !startswith "SANDBOX-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full mshta command line and the downloaded HTA/installer; confirm the domain resolved and returned content (check DeviceNetworkEvents for the same host/time). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all six domains at proxy/DNS, kill mshta and any child python.exe/pythonw.exe. 3) Hunt: search the host for a trojanized installer (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT), a PythonLauncher-* scheduled task, and outbound beacons carrying a C: volume-serial HWID path.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized MobaXterm/WebEx/DBeaver/FaceIT installer spawning Python interpreter AIInstallation High
Hunts UAT-11795 trojanized NSIS installers (MobaXterm_v26.1.exe, WebEx_Client.exe, dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe, FaceitInstaller_x64.exe) spawning python.exe/pythonw.exe, which is the byte-compiled Python loader that decodes and runs Starland RAT in memory. Legitimate versions of these installers do not launch a Python interpreter. Rationale: Parent = the exact trojanized installer filenames from Talos' Table 1, child = python interpreter — legit MobaXterm/WebEx/DBeaver/FaceIT setups never spawn Python, so the parent/child pair is high-fidelity. Corroborated by BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://malware.news/t/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/123963
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer packaging a legitimate Python-bundled build using an identically named installer during testing
  • DBeaver plugin that shells out to a Python helper (rare, usually via javaw not the installer)
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample by an analyst
  • Software-repackaging tools that wrap installers and inject a Python post-install step
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the installer and the python payload; confirm the installer is unsigned/mismatched-signature vs the legitimate vendor build and locate the .pyc loader on disk. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill python/pythonw, quarantine the installer and %TEMP% drops. 3) Hunt: check for follow-on x64/x32 shellcode drops (CastleStealer/Remcos), PythonLauncher-* scheduled task, and C2 beacons to the campaign domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WLDR/Starland persistence: scheduled task named PythonLauncher-{random} AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a scheduled task whose name begins with 'PythonLauncher-' (followed by 3 random characters) via New-ScheduledTask/schtasks — the persistence mechanism UAT-11795 uses to relaunch the Python loader/WLDR agent. The name prefix is a fixed campaign artifact. Rationale: The literal 'PythonLauncher-' task-name prefix (verbatim code block from the article) combined with a task-creation verb is a unique campaign fingerprint with essentially no benign collision. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal automation tool that legitimately names tasks 'PythonLauncher-' (extremely unlikely but verify with the owning team)
  • IR/DFIR teams re-registering the task during controlled detonation
  • EDR replay of the sample in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task XML/action to see the exact python payload path it launches; note the 3-char suffix and creating user. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task, isolate host, kill the launched python/powershell. 3) Hunt: pivot to the payload path for the byte-compiled loader, then check for WLDR PowerShell stager (Runspace engine) and C2 beacons to eorthopaedics.com/sastoro.com /feed/ and /alpha/ paths.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("New-ScheduledTask","Register-ScheduledTask","schtasks","/create")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

Starland/WLDR C2 beacon to UAT-11795 campaign domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network activity to the UAT-11795 C2 and staging domains (eorthopaedics.com, sastoro.com, web-devtools.com, windowscreenrepairnearme.com, aipythondevs.com, zynaris.io). These serve HWID-parameterized C2 envelopes and shellcode; the C: volume-serial HWID forms the final URL path component. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the six campaign domains from the Talos article; DNS/network resolution of any of them is high-fidelity regardless of the HWID path. Domains corroborated via BleepingComputer and OffSeq threat radar. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-dep-e6ab953c0d52f095

Starland RAT Polygon smart-contract fallback C2 resolution via scripting host AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts python/powershell processes reaching Polygon (MATIC) public JSON-RPC endpoints — the mechanism Starland RAT uses to Eth_call the attacker contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba and decrypt an XOR-encoded fallback C2 domain. A Python/PowerShell interpreter contacting a blockchain RPC node is highly anomalous on a corporate endpoint. Rationale: Article states Starland RAT uses a Polygon smart contract (0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba) via Eth_call as a dead-drop C2 resolver; pairing common Polygon RPC hosts with a python/powershell initiator captures that behaviour without needing packet-body inspection of the contract address. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain/Web3 developer running Python (web3.py) or PowerShell scripts against Polygon RPC
  • Crypto-analytics or DeFi tooling installed on a workstation
  • rpc.ankr.com used for non-Polygon chains by a legit app (broadens FP — scope tighten to polygon-* if needed)
  • Security researcher reproducing the Eth_call resolver
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("web3","hardhat","truffle","ethers") and DeviceName in (KnownDevWorkstations)) // maintain a watchlist of sanctioned blockchain dev hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating python/powershell is not a known Web3 dev tool; capture the JSON-RPC request body if proxy/PCAP available and check for the contract address 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba or method eth_call. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the RPC hosts for that endpoint, kill the interpreter. 3) Hunt: decode any XOR fallback domain returned, add it to the C2 blocklist, and check for the primary Starland domains and PythonLauncher-* persistence.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","polygon-mainnet.infura.io","polygon.llamarpc.com","polygon-bor-rpc.publicnode.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon-mainnet.g.alchemy.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","polygon-mainnet.infura.io","polygon.llamarpc.com","polygon-bor-rpc.publicnode.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon-mainnet.g.alchemy.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-11795 Telegram bot beacon (skuefq_bot / komandastuk_bot) from scripting host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound traffic to api.telegram.org carrying the actor-controlled bot IDs 8384531459 (skuefq_bot) or 7993597060 (komandastuk_bot), or any api.telegram.org contact initiated by a Python/PowerShell interpreter. These bots receive Starland/WLDR execution beacons with victim machine fingerprints and crypto-wallet inventories. Rationale: Bot IDs 8384531459 and 7993597060 are exact actor IOCs; where full-URL proxy telemetry exists they give near-zero FP, and the python/powershell-to-api.telegram.org pivot catches the beacon when only host-level DNS/network is available. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://cyberpress.org/uat-11795-spreads-dual-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal automation/monitoring bots posting to Telegram from python/powershell scripts
  • Developer testing a Telegram bot integration
  • IT alerting pipelines that use Telegram as a notification channel
  • Personal Telegram desktop client traffic (would be Telegram.exe, not python — helps distinguish)
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("corp-alert-bot","monitoring") // exclude sanctioned internal Telegram notifier scripts by their known command-line markers
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiator is not a sanctioned internal Telegram-notification script; if full URL is available, verify the bot ID matches 8384531459/7993597060. 2) Contain: block api.telegram.org for the affected host (or the specific bot token at proxy), isolate host, kill the interpreter. 3) Hunt: treat as active data theft — check for CastleStealer/Remcos drops, browser-credential and crypto-wallet file access, and the primary Starland C2 domains on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") or RemoteUrl has_any ("8384531459","7993597060")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "api.telegram.org"
| where Url has_any ("8384531459","7993597060")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

AWS IoT client subscribing to reserved wildcard topic $aws/things/# (Shark vacuum serial harvest) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts a single MQTT principal/certificate subscribing to the reserved wildcard shadow topic $aws/things/# (or /+), the exact reconnaissance step tokay0 used against Shark's IoT broker to enumerate 1.5M device serial numbers. A correctly scoped device only ever subscribes to its own $aws/things/<thingName>/... topics, so a wildcard subscribe to the reserved things namespace is anomalous by definition. Rationale: Uses the article's exact recon string ($aws/things/# wildcard subscribe) — AWS's own IOT_POLICY_OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_CHECK docs confirm subscribing to the reserved things namespace is the abuse pattern, so a single principal doing it is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot-device-defender/latest/devguide/audit-chk-iot-policy-permissive.html • https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/iot/identify-misconfigured-iot-policies-using-aws-iot-device-defender/
ATT&CKT1580 T1078.001
Data sourcesAWS IoT Core logs
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backend fleet-management service intentionally provisioned with a broad subscribe policy (should be an allow-listed service principal, not a device cert)
  • IoT platform monitoring/observability tooling subscribing to reserved topics for diagnostics
  • AWS IoT Device Defender or a SIEM connector using a service certificate to mirror device shadows
  • Load/soak-test harnesses in a non-prod account exercising many things
Suppression filter
| where principalId!="<known-fleet-service-cert>"  -- maintain an allow-list of legitimate backend service certificate IDs
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the clientId/principalId/sourceIp from the hit and confirm whether the principal is a per-device certificate (attacker) or a known backend service cert (likely benign). Check the source IP geolocation/ASN against expected device fleet ranges. 2) Contain: if it is a device certificate, revoke/deactivate that certificate (UpdateCertificate INACTIVE) and detach its policy; the same cert cannot re-subscribe once revoked. 3) Hunt: from that principalId, pull all subsequent Publish/UpdateThingShadow events to enumerate which device shadows it touched, and correlate with the cross-device shadow-write UC.
# log group: AWSIotLogsV2
fields @timestamp, clientId, principalId, sourceIp, eventType, topicName
| filter eventType = "Subscribe"
| filter topicName like /^\$aws\/things\/[#+]/
| stats count(*) as subscribes, count_distinct(topicName) as topics by clientId, principalId, sourceIp
| sort subscribes desc
APPLICATION
index=aws sourcetype="aws:iot" eventType=Subscribe (topicName="$aws/things/#" OR topicName="$aws/things/+" OR topicName="$aws/things/*")
| stats count AS subscribes values(topicName) AS topics min(_time) AS firstSeen by clientId principalId sourceIp
| sort - subscribes
Single AWS IoT principal writing shadows to multiple distinct device thing names (cross-device Exec_Command RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts one MQTT certificate/principal publishing UpdateThingShadow to more than one distinct thing name — the cross-device shadow-write that delivers the Exec_Command field to appd's execute_command()/popen on victim Shark vacuums. A legitimately scoped device only ever writes its own shadow, so any principal addressing multiple thing names is the attack's execution step. Rationale: Directly targets the article's execution primitive (an attacker cert publishing shadow updates carrying Exec_Command to any device topic); the topicName carries the target thingName, so distinct-thing fan-out from one principal is a clean behavioural signature of cross-device control. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot-device-defender/latest/devguide/audit-chk-iot-policy-permissive.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1078.001
Data sourcesAWS IoT Core logs
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate fleet-orchestration backend that pushes shadow updates (jobs, OTA config) to many devices under one service principal — allow-list it
  • A gateway/hub device that proxies shadow state for several child devices it legitimately owns
  • Provisioning tooling bulk-initialising shadows during device onboarding
  • Migration scripts re-writing shadow documents during an account/region move
Suppression filter
| where principalId!="<known-fleet-orchestration-cert>"  -- allow-list legitimate multi-device backend certificate IDs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the principalId and list the distinct thingNames it wrote; if the principal is a per-device certificate but touched multiple thing names, treat as confirmed cross-device control. Inspect (if payload logging/republish rule exists) the shadow document for an Exec_Command field. 2) Contain: deactivate the offending certificate, then push a scoped policy version (CreatePolicyVersion + setAsDefault) pinning topics to ${iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName}; disconnect/quarantine affected thing names. 3) Hunt: for each victim thingName, review outbound NetworkConnectIP/Exec_Response traffic for reverse-shell callbacks and camera-stream egress; pivot on sourceIp across regions for additional certificates.
# log group: AWSIotLogsV2
fields @timestamp, clientId, principalId, sourceIp, eventType, topicName
| filter (eventType = "UpdateThingShadow" or eventType = "Publish")
| filter topicName like /^\$aws\/things\/.+\/shadow\/update$/
| parse topicName "$aws/things/*/shadow/update" as thingName
| stats count_distinct(thingName) as distinctThings, count(*) as writes by clientId, principalId, sourceIp
| filter distinctThings > 1
| sort distinctThings desc
APPLICATION
index=aws sourcetype="aws:iot" (eventType=UpdateThingShadow OR eventType=Publish) topicName="$aws/things/*/shadow/update"
| rex field=topicName "\$aws/things/(?<thingName>[^/]+)/shadow/update"
| stats dc(thingName) AS distinctThings count values(sourceIp) AS srcIps by clientId principalId
| where distinctThings > 1
| sort - distinctThings
AWS IoT policy created/updated granting reserved $aws/things/* topic without ThingName pinning AIWeaponization Medium
Detects CreatePolicy/CreatePolicyVersion CloudTrail events whose policyDocument grants publish/subscribe on the reserved topicfilter/$aws/things/* namespace without the ${iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName} constraint — the exact IOT_POLICY_OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_CHECK shape that made the Shark certificate a region-wide skeleton key. Surfaces the root-cause misconfiguration at provisioning time. Rationale: Encodes AWS's own critical audit finding (IOT_POLICY_OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_CHECK) as a real-time CloudTrail detection using the concrete policyDocument tell (reserved $aws/things/* topicfilter minus the ThingName pin) the article names as the root cause. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot-device-defender/latest/devguide/audit-chk-iot-policy-permissive.html • https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2022/12/aws-iot-device-defender-audit-identifies-potential-misconfiguration-iot-policies/
ATT&CKT1098 T1552.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backend/gateway service policy that intentionally needs broad shadow access (should be explicitly reviewed and allow-listed)
  • Infrastructure-as-code (Terraform/CDK) baseline that ships a permissive template later scoped down
  • Device Defender remediation tooling reissuing a corrected policy (contains ThingName pin — excluded by the filter)
  • Vendor sample/quick-start policy applied in a dev/test account
Suppression filter
| where userIdentity.arn!="<known-iac-provisioning-role-arn>" and requestParameters.policyName!="<approved-backend-service-policy>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the created policyDocument, confirm it grants iot:Subscribe/iot:Receive/iot:Publish on topicfilter/$aws/things/* or resource * with no ${iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName} constraint, and identify which certificates/thing groups it is attached to. 2) Contain: push a scoped replacement with CreatePolicyVersion + setAsDefault (per AWS remediation) so every certificate using the policy is immediately re-scoped; where feasible, reissue affected device certificates. 3) Hunt: run a Device Defender on-demand audit for IOT_POLICY_OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_CHECK across all regions, and review AWSIotLogsV2 for any principal that already exercised the broad grant (wildcard subscribe or cross-device shadow writes).
title: AWS IoT Policy Created With Overly Permissive Reserved Thing Topic
id: 2f9c4e17-6b3a-4d21-9a5e-7c1b0f8e3a44
status: experimental
description: Detects an AWS IoT policy created or versioned that grants access to the reserved $aws/things/* topicfilter without pinning to the connecting thing name, the misconfiguration behind the Shark vacuum region-wide RCE.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-shark-vacuum-flaw-could-let.html
  - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot-device-defender/latest/devguide/audit-chk-iot-policy-permissive.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1098
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: iot.amazonaws.com
    eventName:
      - CreatePolicy
      - CreatePolicyVersion
    requestParameters.policyDocument|contains: 'topicfilter/$aws/things/*'
  filter_scoped:
    requestParameters.policyDocument|contains: 'iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName'
  condition: selection and not filter_scoped
falsepositives:
  - Intentional broad backend/service policies (should be reviewed and allow-listed)
level: high
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(CreatePolicy OR CreatePolicyVersion) @requestParameters.policyDocument:*topicfilter/$aws/things/* -@requestParameters.policyDocument:*iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName*
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.policyName
| filter eventSource = "iot.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["CreatePolicy", "CreatePolicyVersion"]
      and requestParameters.policyDocument like /topicfilter\/\$aws\/things\/\*/
      and not (requestParameters.policyDocument like /iot:Connection\.Thing\.ThingName/)
| sort @timestamp desc
CLOUD
index=aws sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventSource="iot.amazonaws.com" (eventName=CreatePolicy OR eventName=CreatePolicyVersion) requestParameters.policyDocument="*topicfilter/$aws/things/*" NOT requestParameters.policyDocument="*iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName*"
| table _time eventName userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress requestParameters.policyName
| sort - _time

Unpatched Zoom Workplace/VDI/Meeting SDK for Windows (CVE-2026-53412 account-takeover + privesc set) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Windows endpoints whose installed Zoom client is exposed to the July 2026 Zoom advisory CVEs (CVE-2026-53412 unauthenticated network account takeover, plus CVE-2026-53411/53410/53409 local privilege escalation / TOCTOU). This is an exposure-identification hunt driven off the exact CVE IDs from the advisory, not attack detection — none of these flaws were observed exploited in the wild, so the value is prioritising patch remediation of the critical 9.8 client-takeover bug. Rationale: Built entirely on the four concrete CVE IDs published in the Zoom advisory (CVE-2026-53412/53411/53410/53409) and the affected products (Zoom Workplace, VDI Client/Plugin, Meeting SDK, Rooms for Windows) — CVE-ID matching against a maintained vuln feed is zero-false-positive on the identifier itself, and the article states no exploit strings exist to hunt on, so exposure identification is the only high-fidelity option. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/zoom-warns-of-critical-account-takeover-vulnerability/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195454/security/zoom-fixes-cve-2026-53412-a-critical-account-takeover-bug.html • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-53412
ATT&CKT1203 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched but within the MDVM/scanner rescan lag window (up to 24h) so still reported vulnerable
  • Endpoint inside an approved maintenance window scheduled to receive the Zoom update within SLA — not a genuine gap
  • VDI plugin branch-version mismatch: a 6.5.x-branch host on 6.5.18 is fixed even though a naive version compare against 6.6.14 flags it
  • Kiosk/Zoom Rooms appliances managed outside the standard patch pipeline that a vendor handles on its own cadence
  • Third-party scanner mis-fingerprinting a non-Windows or SDK-embedded Zoom component that does not carry the vulnerable client code
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion != RecommendedSecurityUpdate
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each returned DeviceName confirm the actual installed Zoom build against the advisory fixed versions (Zoom Workplace 7.0.5+, VDI Plugin 6.6.14/6.5.17+, Rooms 7.1.0+); deprioritise hosts already above the fix or inside an active patch window. 2) Contain: push the Zoom update via your software-deployment tool to hosts still exposed to the critical CVE-2026-53412, prioritising internet-reachable / high-value users since it is an unauthenticated network account-takeover; where immediate patching is impossible, restrict inbound network exposure to the Zoom client. 3) Hunt: on any host that was exposed, review Zoom client process for anomalous child processes or unexpected outbound connections and check for local privilege-escalation artefacts (unexpected SYSTEM-integrity children of the Zoom installer/updater) to rule out opportunistic abuse of the privesc CVEs.

Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload delivery

Microsoft Security BlogStepSecurity
2026-07-16 18 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors compromised AsyncAPI packages and weaponized trusted CI/CD workflows to distribute malware through npm. This analysis breaks down the attack chain, payload delivery, and recommended defenses. The post Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload delivery appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache · [LLM] Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS gateway (specific CIDs) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload deliv
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Second-stage sync.js dropped under OS 'NodeJS' masquerade directory · [LLM] Detached hidden node.exe executing sync.js from NodeJS masquerade path
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to Miasma controller 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache AIDelivery High
Hunts for the five backdoored @asyncapi package versions (@asyncapi/specs 6.11.2 & 6.11.2-alpha.1, generator 3.3.1, generator-components 0.7.1, generator-helpers 1.1.1) landing on developer/CI hosts via npm or Yarn dependency resolution. Article-specific because it pins the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft/Socket confirmed, not generic 'npm install' activity. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft published and Socket/StepSecurity independently confirmed; package name is always lowercase in the registry/cache so no casing enumeration needed, and version+name combined is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or IR teams intentionally downloading the malicious versions into a sandbox for analysis
  • An internal mirror/Artifactory that cached the bad versions during the exposure window and is now being audited
  • Developers who pinned 6.11.2 in a lockfile and re-ran install against a still-poisoned private proxy
  • Yarn/npm cache directories restored from an old backup image containing the version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","yarn.exe","npm-cli.js") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("malware-analysis","sandbox","detonate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path is a real install target (node_modules, .yarn/cache, npm _cacache) and not a knowingly-collected sample; capture the host, user, and whether it's a dev box or CI runner. 2) Contain: isolate the host, purge npm & Yarn caches, remove all five affected versions, and pin @asyncapi/specs to a known-good release; block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 at egress. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to a detached node child writing sync.js under the NodeJS masquerade dir and any outbound IPFS fetch; rotate every credential reachable from that environment (npm tokens, GitHub CLI, AWS, SSH keys).

| where (FileName has "specs" and FileName has "6.11.2")
    or (FileName has "generator-helpers" and FileName has "1.1.1")
    or (FileName has "generator-components" and FileName has "0.7.1")
    or (FileName has "generator" and FileName has "3.3.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where (TargetFileName has "specs" and TargetFileName has "6.11.2")

    or (TargetFileName has "generator" and TargetFileName has "3.3.1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
